item.title: Sharing a Workspace
item.description:
Share designs from Workspaces 🔗

Five has been working in the orbital-dev workspace — a development sandbox with a local Kubernetes environment (kind) and LocalStack for AWS service emulation. Rex Park, a developer on the Orbital Labs Development team, needs access so he can deploy the microservices-baseline design and test his service changes without touching staging.

Here is how Five shares the orbital-dev workspace with Rex.

item.title: Promoting a Design from Staging to Prod
item.description:
This guide walks through how Five promotes the prod-deployment-v2 design from the orbital-staging workspace to orbital-production, with Zara Osei (Infrastructure Team Admin) approving the environment assignment.

See Meet Five and the Cast for the full Orbital Labs narrative reference.

Overview 🔗

At Orbital Labs, workspaces mirror the deployment pipeline:

Workspace Environment Teams with Access
orbital-staging staging-aws (EKS + S3 + ElastiCache), staging-azure (AKS + Azure Blob + Azure Service Bus) Infrastructure + Development
orbital-production prod-aws (EKS + RDS + S3 + CloudFront + SQS), prod-gcp (GKE + Cloud SQL + Cloud Storage + Pub/Sub) Infrastructure only

Five has finished validating prod-deployment-v2 in staging. The design deploys an EKS cluster, an RDS PostgreSQL database, an S3 bucket, and a CloudFront distribution — the core of Orbital Labs’ AWS production platform.

item.title: Recognizing User and Contributor Milestones
item.description:
Layer5 badges are one of the many ways that we recognize the efforts of our contributors and uplift our users. Layer5 badges represent milestones that you achieve both in using and in contributing to Layer5-supported open source projects. As a contributor, this is how you demonstrate your ownership, dedication, skills and loyalty to Layer5. As a user, this is how you demonstrate your prowess.

Info

See all Achievement and all Project badges in the Badge Gallery.

How to Earn Badges 🔗

Earning Layer5 badges is both rewarding and straightforward. Each badge is tied to specific activities. For users, badges for activities such as using our projects, talking about the projects, sharing your successes and what you like about them. For contributors, badges include activities such as submitting code, assisting with documentation, participating in community events, and more. As you accumulate contributions in various areas, you’ll begin to unlock badges that showcase your multifaceted involvement.

item.title: Collaborative Editing
item.description: In this tutorial, you and a teammate work on the same design at the same time. You save a design, share it, watch your teammate join as a live collaborator, edit together, and run a short review in a comment thread. Along the way you learn the four separate mechanisms behind collaboration in Kanvas: the live session, access, comments, and saving. Each one explains a different part of what you see.

item.title: Explore Pods
item.description: In this tutorial you build a single NGINX Pod in Kanvas, deploy it to a live cluster, expose it with a NodePort Service, and inspect the running Pod in Operator: its details, a shell inside its container, and its log stream. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and every workload controller you meet later (Deployments, StatefulSets, CronJobs) exists to create and replace Pods. Working with a bare Pod first shows you exactly what those controllers automate.

item.title: Share a Design Across Organizations
item.description: In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.

item.title: Explore Deployments
item.description: In this tutorial you build an NGINX Deployment with two replicas, deploy it, scale it to three, and roll it to a new image version, inspecting the result in Operator after each change. A Deployment is the controller most stateless applications run under: you declare how many Pods you want and what they look like, and Kubernetes keeps that many running and replaces them gradually when the template changes. Seeing the ReplicaSets and Pods appear and change shows you what the controller does on your behalf.

item.title: Tutorials
item.description:
A Kanvas tutorial is a guided path to a realistic outcome. You build something real, such as a shared design, a cloud architecture, or a running application, and you learn how Kanvas works by doing it. Each tutorial explains what Kanvas does at every step, so you finish with both the result and the mental model behind it.

Tutorials are for learning. When you already know what you want to do, other parts of the Kanvas docs serve you better:

item.title: Build a GCP Data Pipeline Design
item.description: In this tutorial you follow Zara Osei, Team Admin of the Orbital Labs Infrastructure Team, as she models the team’s Google Cloud data pipeline in Kanvas. The pipeline ingests events through Pub/Sub, processes them with Dataflow, writes analytical results to BigQuery, archives raw payloads to Cloud Storage, and runs alongside a GKE cluster. The result is a design named data-pipeline-gcp: a reviewable, shareable model of the architecture that lives in the team’s workspace instead of in a slide deck.

item.title: Explore Services
item.description: In this tutorial you put three Services in front of running workloads: a ClusterIP Service in front of a Deployment, a NodePort Service in front of one Pod, and a LoadBalancer Service in front of another. Pods come and go and change IP addresses every time they are replaced. A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable address and finds them by label, and its type decides who can reach that address. Building all three side by side makes the difference between the types concrete.

item.title: Use ConfigMaps and Secrets
item.description: In this tutorial you design a MySQL Pod that takes its database name from a ConfigMap and its root password from a Secret, deploy it to a cluster, and prove from inside the container that each value arrived. Separating configuration and credentials from the container image is how one image runs unchanged in every environment, and knowing exactly how Kubernetes delivers those values tells you why a changed setting sometimes reaches a running container and sometimes does not.

item.title: Deploy AWS EC2 Instances
item.description: In this tutorial you create a VPC network and EC2 instances in your AWS account without leaving Kanvas. You deploy three designs from the catalog, in order, to your own Kubernetes cluster: a controller that talks to AWS, a VPC network, and the EC2 instances that run inside it. Each AWS resource is a Kubernetes custom resource in the design, and a controller in the cluster turns that resource into real infrastructure.

item.title: Schedule Work with CronJobs
item.description: In this tutorial you design a CronJob that runs a small container every minute, deploy it, and watch Kubernetes turn the schedule into Jobs and the Jobs into Pods. Then you change the schedule in place and clean up. Scheduled work such as backups, report generation, and cache warming runs this way, and understanding the CronJob to Job to Pod chain is what lets you answer the two questions that matter in production: did it run, and where is its output.

item.title: Deploy Azure Resources
item.description:
In this tutorial you install Azure Service Operator (ASO) in your own Kubernetes cluster, then design an Azure resource group and a storage account inside it, deploy both from Kanvas, and find them in the Azure portal. You manage real Azure infrastructure with the same design, validate, and deploy loop you use for Kubernetes workloads, and the cluster keeps that infrastructure matched to the design.

The trade-off is indirection. Kanvas never calls Azure. It applies Kubernetes objects to your cluster, and ASO turns those objects into Azure resources in the background. A successful deploy means the cluster accepted the objects; the Azure resources follow a little later, and Azure-side failures surface on the objects in the cluster, not in the deploy summary.

item.title: Kubernetes Tutorials
item.description:
These tutorials teach core Kubernetes objects by building them in Kanvas, deploying them to a live cluster, and inspecting the result. Each one ends with real objects running in a cluster, so you learn both the Kubernetes concept and the Kanvas workflow that takes a design from the canvas to the cluster and back into view.

The learning path 🔗

Work through the tutorials in order. The first five each introduce one kind of object. The last three combine many objects into complete applications and assume you know the earlier material.

item.title: Deploy a PHP Guestbook with Redis
item.description: In this tutorial you build the Kubernetes guestbook: a PHP frontend that writes entries to a Redis leader and reads them from Redis followers. Six manifests from the Kubernetes examples become one Kanvas design, which you deploy, inspect in Operator, scale, and remove. The application is small, but it carries the pattern behind most multi-tier systems: each tier runs as a Deployment, each tier is reached through a Service, and tiers find each other by Service name, never by Pod address.

item.title: Deploy WordPress and MySQL with Persistent Volumes
item.description: In this tutorial you deploy WordPress backed by a MySQL database, and you give both tiers storage that outlives their Pods. You import the two Kubernetes example manifests into one design, add the Secret that holds the database password, and add the PersistentVolumes that the claims bind to. Stateless Pods can be replaced at any moment; a database cannot lose its files when that happens. This tutorial shows how Kubernetes separates the data from the Pod, and exactly which pieces a deploy creates and an undeploy removes.

item.title: Deploy Cassandra with a StatefulSet
item.description: In this tutorial you deploy Apache Cassandra as a three-node ring. A Deployment treats its Pods as interchangeable; Cassandra cannot, because each node owns part of the data and other nodes must find it at a known address. A StatefulSet gives every replica a fixed ordinal, a fixed DNS name, and its own volume, and starts the replicas one at a time. You import the Kubernetes example manifests into a Kanvas design, adapt them to your cluster, deploy, and watch the ring form.
